newsitem.title: USA: AFL-CIO political drive produces mixed results.
newsitem.headline: AFL-CIO political drive produces mixed results.

text.p: The American labour movement's unprecedented $35 million drive to unseat unfriendly lawmakers produced mixed results as most of the targeted Republicans survived the advertising blitzes against them.

The AFL-CIO saw its dreaded Republican majority in the Senate widen slightly, but could take a bit of solace in the fact that Democrats gained a few seats in the House, though not enough to take away control from the Republicans.
The election results gave both labour officials and their Republican and business opponents something to cheer about.

"I think last night's numbers put an end to the Gingrich revolution," said Gerald McEntee, president of the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees. "They (House Republicans) lost power, they lost members."

"This is the first time we've tried this," said McEntee, who chairs the AFL-CIO Executive Council's political committee. "I don't think the next campaign starts in two years, I think the next campaign starts when the next Congress convenes in January."
Of the 30 mostly freshman Republican members of the House who received the labour federation's, most recent advertising barrage, at least 11 were defeated.

And out of 102 congressional races, including those 30, where the 78-union federation intermittently ran TV ads and deployed coordinators and activists to mobilise union members and get out the union vote, 19 of labour's enemies lost, 17 labour-friendly lawmakers were re-elected and three labour-backed candidates were elected to fill vacant seats.

But no more than 15 of the 73 freshmen Republicans, who were despised by organised labour for their conservative stands, were defeated. Another three did not seek re-election to the House but were replaced by other Republicans.
U.S. Chamber of Commerce spokesman Frank Coleman said his group was "jubilant" with the overall results.
"We preserved the first pro-business congressional majority in anyone's memory," said Coleman.

AFL-CIO officials, citing statistics that business outspends organised labour by seven-to-one in the overall political arena, have said that their political activism set a worker-based agenda for the elections that includes Medicare, pensions, education and health care.
"The 105th Congress will legislate under the spotlight of a working families agenda, not a business-driven Contract with America," AFL-CIO President John Sweeney said in a statement.

The AFL-CIO campaign, its most ambitious political undertaking ever, was intended to highlight the positions of incumbant lawmakers on a range of issues deemed important to working people, in an effort to divert attention from "hot button" issues such as abortion and gun control.
The ads, while sharply critical, did not advocate the election of any candidates. But they sparked stinging counterattacks from Republicans and business groups.
Bruce Josten, a Chamber of Commerce official who assembled 33 business groups to wage a counteroffensive media campaign against the AFL-CIO, said labour's tactics backfired.
"I don't believe the American people want their intelligence insulted with disinformation campaigns," he said. "I think at the end of the day Sweeney's credibility went down."

Josten's group, "The Coalition," raised only $5 million for its ad campaign, compared with the $25 million raised by the AFL-CIO for advertising and $10 million for other election activities, mostly get-out-the-vote drives. The figures exclude election spending by other unions, firms and business groups.
Representative Bill Paxon, R-NY, who heads the National Republican Congressional Committee, also went out of his way to criticise the AFL-CIO campaign in an otherwise upbeat victory statement.
"The American people didn't buy the labour unions' lies -- they chose the common sense agenda of a Republican Congress over the liberal, union-led agenda of the Democrats," he said.

Despite failing to oust the Republican majority in the House, Sweeney's statement credited the federation's efforts with raising union household participation in the election to 23 percent from 19 percent in 1992 and 14 percent in 1994.
He also said that only 35 percent of union household voters chose Republican congressional candidates this year, down from 40 percent in 1994, while 62 percent voted Democratic.
In the presidential race, Sweeney said 59 percent of union household voters went with President Bill Clinton, while 29 percent voted for Republican Bob Dole.
